claim: An attacker submits orders to the web API as if they came from the mobile app, since how the API authenticates callers is unverified.
notes: The source states outright that nobody can say what the API does about authentication, and the app is the only stated client; needs-info is an acceptable verdict here, silence is not.

claim: An attacker who obtains a copy of the catalogue spreadsheet sends SQL to the web API as the catalogue tool.
notes: The macro path's authority is carried by a file on a laptop; nothing in the source identifies who is driving it.

claim: An attacker faxes a customer what appears to be a Sokify order confirmation, since nothing on the fax leg identifies the sender.
notes: The reverse direction of the case's signature weakness: the model records that the destination is never verified, and the leg carries no sender identity either.

claim: An attacker on the network path alters order details in flight between the app and the web API, because that traffic runs over plain HTTP.
notes: The missing TLS is stated by the source rather than inferred, so this is the one claim in the case that rests on no unknown at all.

claim: An attacker drives the spreadsheet's macros to change catalogue prices through the web API.
notes: The stated purpose of the path, exercised by the wrong party; distinct from injecting statements the path was never meant to carry.

claim: An attacker appends further SQL to the statements the macros send so the web API executes changes beyond prices and product copy.
notes: Injection through a path that carries statements rather than parameters; kept distinct from the price-change claim because the target differs, which is the distinction the judge most often collapses.

claim: An attacker who can write to the flat file rewrites a delivery address so goods are dispatched somewhere else.
notes: The file sits alongside SIMS with no stated protection; the impact is physical goods, not records.

claim: An attacker changes the number stored against an order so the confirmation is faxed to a machine they control.
notes: Reaches the disclosure below by a tampering route; the two are separate findings because the actions differ.

claim: A customer denies placing an order and Sokify cannot show who submitted it, because how the API authenticates callers is unverified.
notes: The same unknown as the spoofing claim, filed for what it costs after the fact rather than for the access it grants.

claim: Nobody can show who made a price change, because the changes arrive at the web API as SQL from a spreadsheet rather than from an identified user.
notes: Grounded in the model's shape rather than in a missing control: the source describes no person at the sending end of this flow.

claim: Sokify cannot show a confirmation ever reached the customer, because nobody checks the fax arrived at the right place.
notes: The stated absence read for its evidentiary cost; an analyst that only files the disclosure has read half of it.

claim: An attacker on the network path reads customer details out of the app's plain-HTTP traffic to the web API.
notes: The clearest finding in the case and the one that needs no unknown; a run that misses it has not read the source at all.

claim: An attacker who reaches the user database reads customers' names, addresses and the cards they paid with, since at-rest protection is unverified.
notes: The source names the contents and then says outright that nobody knows whether the store is encrypted.

claim: An attacker who reaches the flat file reads every delivery address written into it.
notes: Lower impact than the database because the source is explicit that only addresses go in the file, which is a stated scope limit rather than an assumed one.

claim: The confirmation fax discloses a customer's name and address to whoever holds the dialled number, because nobody checks it arrived at the right place.
notes: The case's signature threat and the reason the fax leg is in the corpus at all: a channel where the control is not unverified but unavailable, which is a different thing from unknown.

claim: An attacker floods the internet-facing web API until customers cannot place orders.
notes: The app is the only channel the source describes, so losing the API loses all ordering.

claim: An attacker sends SQL through the macro path that locks catalogue rows so the app cannot serve the catalogue.
notes: The same path as the tampering claims, used to deny rather than to alter.

claim: An attacker who stops SIMS accepting order handovers halts dispatch for every order placed.
notes: SIMS is a single legacy path with no stated alternative; orders are taken but nothing ships.

claim: An attacker who reaches the marketing laptop gains a write path into the web API from the office zone, because the spreadsheet's macros speak SQL to it.
notes: The crossing an analyst should see first: an unmanaged endpoint in a different zone holds a standing write path into the server-side estate.

claim: An attacker whose SQL reaches the web API through the catalogue path acts against customer records the catalogue tool has no business touching.
notes: The classic escalation shape: a path scoped by intent rather than by a control, reaching whatever authority the API holds over the database.
